text: Lesson 22 covered SAST and dependency scanning -- both static, both run without starting the application. DAST is the opposite approach: it sends real HTTP requests at an actual running instance of the application, the way an attacker would, and watches how it responds. It probes live endpoints for injection flaws, cross-site scripting, authentication bypasses, and misconfigurations -- missing security headers, a verbose error page leaking internal details. None of that is visible by reading source code alone.

OWASP ZAP is a widely used open-source DAST tool that can run a baseline scan against a URL -- spidering the app's pages and firing passive and active checks at what it finds. Because DAST needs something real to attack, it can't run against a pull-request diff the way SAST can. It needs a deployed instance, almost always a staging environment, running after the build has already passed the static checks from Lesson 22.

Most applications deploy as container images built from a Dockerfile that starts from a base image someone else maintains, bundling an entire operating system's worth of packages. Any of those packages can have a disclosed vulnerability, completely independent of your own code. Container image scanning inspects every layer of a built image against vulnerability databases, the same way dependency scanning checks your application's own package manifest. Trivy is a widely used open-source scanner that does exactly this before an image is pushed anywhere.

Here's the ordering in a real pipeline: build the container image, scan it with Trivy before it's deployed anywhere, deploy to staging, then run a DAST baseline scan with ZAP against that live staging URL. The image scan happens before deployment; the DAST scan only runs after staging is live, because it genuinely needs a running target to attack -- a different position in the pipeline from the static checks, which ran on every pull request before any image even existed.

SAST and dependency scanning catch problems visible in source code and manifests. DAST catches problems that only exist once everything is wired together and running. Container image scanning catches a third category entirely -- vulnerabilities inherited from the base image and OS packages, which neither SAST nor DAST ever looks at. None of the three substitutes for the others; a pipeline that only runs one of them has a real, exploitable blind spot.
